screens.title: Out of balance
screens.text: A has just been inserted, and node G now has a balance factor of −2. How would you fix it?
options: Sort all the keys and rebuild the tree
Lift C up and let G move down
screens.answer: Lift C up and let G move down
screens.reveal: Rebuilding from sorted keys works, but it needs sorting every time a key is added. A rotation fixes the balance locally, by moving a child up and its parent down, without breaking the BST order.

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify and perform the single or double rotation to restore AVL balance.

task.stem: An in-order traversal of a BST lists the keys in which order?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can verify a result. The in-order keys must still be sorted, and every balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.

options.explanation: That is why an in-order check can show that a rotation kept the BST order.

options.text: The order in which they were inserted
options.explanation: In-order means the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. This gives sorted order, whatever the insertion order was.

options.text: Level by level, from the root down
options.explanation: That is a breadth-first, or level-order, traversal.

screens.title: Right rotation, step by step
screens.text: A single rotation swaps the roles of a child and its parent without breaking the BST order. Here the child C (30) rotates around its parent P (50), whose own parent is G (80).
screens.caption: In a right rotation, the parent becomes the right child of its left child.
steps: Rotate 30 around 50. This is a right rotation about 50.
roleSteps: 1. The grandparent G (80) of the child C (30) becomes the parent of C, replacing P (50).
2. The right subtree of C, which is 40, becomes the left subtree of P (50).
3. C (30) takes P (50) as its right child.

screens.title: Left rotation
screens.text: This is the mirror image. The child 40 rotates around its parent 20.
screens.caption: In a left rotation, the parent becomes the left child of its right child.
steps: Rotate 40 around 20. This is a left rotation about 20.
roleSteps: 1. 40 takes the place of 20 at the top of this subtree.
2. The left subtree of 40, which is 30, becomes the right subtree of 20.

screens.title: The four cases
points: In Case 1 (LL), the new key is in the left subtree of the left child of n. The fix is a right rotation about n.
In Case 2 (LR), the new key is in the right subtree of the left child of n. The fix is a left rotation about n.left, followed by a right rotation about n.
In Case 3 (RL), the new key is in the left subtree of the right child of n. The fix is a right rotation about n.right, followed by a left rotation about n.
In Case 4 (RR), the new key is in the right subtree of the right child of n. The fix is a left rotation about n.
Cases 1 and 4 are on the “outside” and need one rotation. Cases 2 and 3 are on the “inside” and need two rotations, which together are called a double rotation.
screens.showRule: The outside cases (LL and RR) need a single rotation. The inside cases (LR and RL) need a double rotation.

screens.title: Case 1: one right rotation
screens.text: This is the opening tree again. A went into the left subtree of C, the left child of G, so this is Case 1.
screens.caption: Rotate C around G. This is a single right rotation about the unbalanced node.
steps: A is smaller than G, so A goes left.
A is smaller than C, so A goes left.
A is smaller than B, so A goes left.
A goes into the empty left branch of B.
Node B now has a balance factor of −1 − 0 = −1.
Node C now has a balance factor of 0 − 1 = −1.
Node G now has a balance factor of 0 − 2 = −2.
Node G has a balance factor of −2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 1 (LL).
Rotate C around G. This is a right rotation about G.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Why one rotation is not always enough
screens.text: Here E went into the right subtree of C, the left child of G, so this is Case 2, an inside case. Watch what a single right rotation does.
screens.caption: The single rotation only moves the problem, because C now has a balance factor of +2.
steps: Rotate C around G. This is a right rotation about G.

screens.title: Case 2: the double rotation
screens.text: First, a left rotation about n.left, which is C, turns Case 2 into Case 1. Then a right rotation about n, which is G, fixes the tree.
screens.caption: Rotate D around C, and then rotate D around G.
steps: Rotate D around C. This is a left rotation about C.
Rotate D around G. This is a right rotation about G.

task.stem: 6 has just been inserted, and the tree is out of balance. Select the unbalanced node and choose the rotation that fixes it.
task.hint: This question checks whether you can carry out the rotation or rotations. The child moves up around its parent, and the child's inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Rotate towards the shorter branch. If n's left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation. If n's right branch is too tall, it is a left rotation.
Fix the first unbalanced node on the way up from the new key. That node is 8, not the root.

feedback.correct: Node 8 is n, with a balance factor of −2. 6 went into the left subtree of the left child of 8, so this is Case 1, and a single right rotation about 8 fixes it. The textbook shows this example in Figure 4.32.
feedback.incorrect: Node 8 is n, with a balance factor of −2. 6 went into the left subtree of the left child of 8, so this is Case 1, and a single right rotation about 8 fixes it. The textbook shows this example in Figure 4.32.

task.stem: 15 has just been inserted. Find n and perform the rotation or rotations.
task.hint: This question checks whether you can carry out the rotation or rotations. The child moves up around its parent, and the child's inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: For an inside case, rotate about n's child first, which turns it into an outside case. Then rotate about n.
Rotate towards the shorter branch. If n's left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation. If n's right branch is too tall, it is a left rotation.
Fix the first unbalanced node on the way up from the new key. That node is 7, not the root.

feedback.correct: Node 7 is n, with a balance factor of +2. 15 went into the left subtree of 16, the right child of 7, so this is Case 3. The fix is a right rotation about 16, followed by a left rotation about 7. This is the textbook's running example.
feedback.incorrect: Node 7 is n, with a balance factor of +2. 15 went into the left subtree of 16, the right child of 7, so this is Case 3. The fix is a right rotation about 16, followed by a left rotation about 7. This is the textbook's running example.

task.stem: Here is the tree after your rotations. How can you check that it is correct?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can verify a result. The in-order keys must still be sorted, and every balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.

options.text: Check that the in-order keys are still sorted and that every balance factor is −1, 0 or +1.
options.explanation: A rotation must keep the BST order and restore the AVL rule.

options.text: Check only that the in-order keys are still sorted.
options.explanation: Sorted in-order keys show that the BST order is kept, but not that the tree is balanced.

options.text: Check only the balance factor of the root.
options.explanation: Every node must have a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1, not just the root.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: This check has one question for each assessment criterion of the lesson's objective. You can re-attempt each question once, and the Hint button is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: A rotation moves a child up around its parent and keeps the in-order sequence.
The outside cases (1 and 4) need one rotation, and the inside cases (2 and 3) need two.
Always check the result. The in-order keys must still be sorted, and every balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.
